name: Felix Kowalski

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello Felix, thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent research group, with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you tell me is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I lead a formwork gang, five of us, on a seven-storey block of flats going up by the old cotton mill. Formwork is the wooden and steel moulds we build so the concrete has a shape when it's poured, so my day is plywood, props and a lot of shouting over the pump. I check every shutter before the pour, because if one blows out you've got four tonnes of wet concrete on the floor and a very angry engineer. I like the pour itself, the whole crew working like one animal. What wears me out is the cold in the mornings and the paperwork that keeps getting longer.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What's home like, and how are things with money?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Irena and I have been married thirty-one years. She's a home care worker, out all hours, and our daughter Ola is a nurse two towns over with a baby boy. Money is tight, I'll be straight with you. We gave Ola most of what we had for her flat deposit last year, so there's maybe two or three weeks in the account, and the firm here pays less than the big contractors in the city, but the city is an hour and a half each way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now I'll read you five pictures of the future, one at a time. The first is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, now let's talk about the things that actually matter on site, like pay and safety. I'd probably post something like that in the union group chat. The lads would make jokes about the robot that never came.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I carry on and slowly rebuild the savings we gave Ola. Seven, eight years more on the tools if my back holds. I do use the AI thing on my phone sometimes, to translate for Bogdan who's still learning English, so I'd keep that, it's handy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as now. I'd keep running the gang, go back to putting a hundred a month aside, and keep going to the union meetings on the first Tuesday. Maybe I'd look again at the city contractors, for the better rate, if the trains get better.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Like a normal Monday, nothing special.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned translating for Bogdan. How did you start doing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ola showed me at Christmas. Bogdan didn't understand a method statement, the safety plan for a job, and I typed it in and it came out in Polish. I checked it with my own Polish, which is rusty, and it was mostly right. Now I use it once a week maybe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the hundred a month be for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A cushion first, because three weeks is nothing. Then one day a trip to Kraków with Irena to see where my father grew up. We keep saying next year.

S0.say: He'd say good, now let's talk about the real issues on site like pay and safety, probably in the union chat. The crew would joke about the robot that never came.
S0.think: Privately it means carrying on and rebuilding the savings they gave their daughter, with seven or eight years left on the tools. He'd keep using the phone translator for his crew.
S0.do: Keeps running the formwork gang and goes back to saving about a hundred a month. Keeps attending monthly union meetings and looks again at better-paid city contractors if transport improves.
S0.quote: I typed it in and it came out in Polish. I checked it with my own Polish, which is rusty, and it was mostly right.
S0.fieldNote: He uses AI in a small, practical way, checking it against his own knowledge before trusting it. His low savings come from generosity, a deposit for his daughter, not poor planning. The plateau changes almost nothing for him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the union needs to get ahead of it, not fight it after. Sit down with the firms now and agree how the change happens: training, no sackings without consultation, older workers not thrown on the scrap heap. That's what I'd say at the meeting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I think formwork is in the middle. The design and the ordering side will go to computers, and maybe the rebar tying, but building a shutter on a muddy slab in the wind, that's harder for a machine. I'd be all right, probably, but the young ones in my gang might get fewer hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Once I'd seen it working on other sites, I'd learn whatever the new setting-out kit is, the laser and tablet stuff, so I'm the one who runs it. I'd ask the union for a course and I'd take it in the evenings if I had to. And I'd keep putting the hundred a month by, maybe a bit more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A little uneasy, but not frightened. It's like when they brought in the system formwork, the metal panels, years ago. We grumbled and then we learned.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd wait until you'd seen it working. What would convince you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If I saw a gang on another job using it for a few months without disasters, without the engineer rejecting the pour. I'm not the first one in the water, but I'm not the last either. I went on the phone translator only after Ola showed me it worked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who in your gang would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Kemal. He's forty, good hands, but he can't read well, and if everything becomes tablets and screens he'll struggle. I'd want the union course to be done with pictures and practice, not exams.

S1.say: He'd tell the union to get ahead of the change by agreeing training, consultation before job cuts, and protection for older workers with the firms now.
S1.think: Privately he thinks formwork sits in the middle: design and ordering go to computers, but building shutters on a muddy slab is hard for machines. His younger crew may lose hours.
S1.do: Learns the new setting-out kit once it has proven itself on other sites, taking a union course in the evenings if needed. Keeps saving a hundred a month or a little more.
S1.feel: A little uneasy but not frightened, like when metal formwork panels first came in.
S1.quote: It's like when they brought in the system formwork, the metal panels, years ago. We grumbled and then we learned.
S1.fieldNote: He trusts change once he has seen it work, and draws on past changes in the trade to stay steady. His worry shifts quickly to Kemal, a crew member with poor reading. He wants union training made practical rather than exam-based.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a disaster made by people who never stood on a slab, and the government has to step in hard. Tax the companies, pay people while it shakes out. I'd be at every union rally and I'd say it loudly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately it means I'm out within two years and the savings are gone in three weeks. At fifty-eight in this town, there's nothing else, there's the supermarket warehouse and that'll have robots too. Irena's care work might last longer, people still want a hand to hold, but on her wage alone we can't cover the rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to the union the first week and get on whatever committee is negotiating redundancy terms. I'd sell the second car, it's worth maybe two thousand, and stop everything that isn't food and rent. And I'd ask the council about housing help early, before the queue gets long.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened. I don't sleep well already, and this would be every night at three in the morning, staring at the ceiling.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does two years of warning give you anything to work with?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit. Two years, I'd take every overtime shift going and put all of it away, maybe four or five thousand if I'm lucky. That's a few months of rent, not a plan. It buys time to get a place in the queue, that's all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about Ola? Would you lean on her?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. Not after we just helped her with the flat, and she has a baby. If anything I'd worry the robots come for nursing too and she needs us. I'd rather go without than take from her.

S2.say: He'd call it a disaster made by people who've never stood on a slab, demand the government tax the companies and support workers, and be at every union rally.
S2.think: Privately he expects to be out within two years with savings that last three weeks, at 58 in a town with no other work. His wife's care job alone can't cover the rent.
S2.do: Joins the union committee negotiating redundancy terms in the first week and sells the second car for about two thousand. Takes every overtime shift during the two years to save a few thousand and asks the council about housing help early.
S2.feel: Frightened and losing sleep, staring at the ceiling at three in the morning.
S2.quote: Maybe four or five thousand if I'm lucky. That's a few months of rent, not a plan.
S2.fieldNote: He moves into practical damage control fast, with the union, the car sale and the council queue. He refuses to lean on his daughter even though he gave her his savings. The anger is aimed at decision-makers far from the site.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a chance, so let's not waste it arguing whether it's real. Get the deals done now. Retraining, a pension bridge, and the robot companies paying for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's still very hard but it's not hopeless. Five years puts me at sixty-three. If I can stay on the tools until then, maybe on the last bits of work the robots can't handle yet, I'm close to the pension. And I'd want the union to win something for workers like me in the middle.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first couple of years, once it was clear, I'd get trained on the robot formwork systems, so I'm the one supervising them, not the one replaced by them. I'd use the AI more, to learn, not just to translate. And I'd save like mad, sell the second car, and talk to Irena about moving somewhere smaller in year four.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but I'd have my hands on the wheel. That's a different feeling from just falling.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Moving somewhere smaller. Is that something you've talked about before?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Irena raised it after Ola moved out. I said no, I like the garden. In this picture I'd say yes, a flat near the bus station, cheaper rent, and I'd miss the tomatoes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the most useful thing the extra three years gives you, compared with the two-year picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Time to watch it come and get on the right side of it. With two years I'm just bailing water. With five, I can see which sites get the robots first and learn from the gangs that go through it before me.

S3.say: He'd say five years is a chance not to be wasted arguing, and push for retraining, a pension bridge and the robot firms paying for it.
S3.think: Privately it's hard but not hopeless, since five years brings him to 63 and near the pension if he can stay on the last work robots can't do. He wants the union to win something for workers his age.
S3.do: Gets trained on robotic formwork once it's clearly coming so he can supervise it, and uses AI to learn. Saves hard, sells the second car and plans with his wife to move to a cheaper flat in year four.
S3.feel: Worried but in control, with his hands on the wheel instead of falling.
S3.quote: Worried, but I'd have my hands on the wheel. That's a different feeling from just falling.
S3.fieldNote: Five years lets his steady approach work: watch others go first, then learn. Agreeing to give up the garden he loves shows how seriously he takes it. The union remains his main frame.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's no excuse with ten years. If the government and firms can't plan with a decade's notice, they never will. I'd push in the union for the young ones to start retraining now, paid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be sixty-eight. I'd plan to work to sixty-six, so for me it's mostly about whether I can last the distance, not whether the robots get me. My grandson would be ten, and that's who I'd think about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on with the gang and keep saving. I'd take the robot training when it's offered, maybe in year five or six, once it's proven, so I can finish my last years as the supervisor. And I'd tell Kemal and the young ones to start learning now, while they've got time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly fine for me. Uneasy for the boys in the gang, and for my grandson.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Kemal to learn?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The maintenance side, fixing the machines, or the inspection side, checking the work. Somebody still signs off the pour. I'd tell him to start with reading, honestly, I'd help him myself on lunch breaks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does ten years change how you feel about the robots themselves?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit. With ten years, they arrive slowly enough that we can make the rules first. I'm not against machines, I'm against people being thrown away.

S4.say: He'd say there's no excuse with a decade's notice and push the union to get younger workers into paid retraining now.
S4.think: Privately at 68 he'd be past his planned retirement, so the question is lasting the distance, not losing to robots. He thinks mostly of his grandson.
S4.do: Carries on leading the gang and saving, and takes robot training around year five or six once it's proven. Urges younger crew to retrain now and offers to help Kemal with reading at lunch.
S4.feel: Mostly fine for himself, uneasy for his crew and his grandson.
S4.quote: I'm not against machines, I'm against people being thrown away.
S4.fieldNote: With ten years his concern turns outward to his crew and grandson. He separates machines from how workers are treated, which sums up his politics. The offer to teach Kemal to read on lunch breaks was unprompted.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. No time to save, no time to learn, and I'm at the wrong age for everything. What would help is the union having a seat at the table from day one, and some payment to carry men like me to the pension, paid for by the companies making the money.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the safety side. A robot that makes a mistake on a pour can kill someone underneath. Whoever brings them on site, there needs to be a person with experience watching, and I'd like that person to be one of us.

headlineQuote: Irena's care work might last longer, people still want a hand to hold, but on her wage alone we can't cover the rent.
portrait: Felix Kowalski is a 58-year-old formwork gang leader on a block of flats in a mill town, with two or three weeks of savings after helping his daughter with a deposit. He is a steady union man who adopts new tools once he has seen them work, like the phone translator he uses for a crew member. Plateau and steady change feel manageable to him, but AGI in two years leaves him sleepless and selling the car. Five years lets him plan to supervise the robots and move somewhere cheaper, and ten years turns his worry towards his crew and his grandson.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, because there's no time to save or learn and he's at the wrong age for everything.
whatWouldHelp: A union seat at the table from the start and a payment to carry older workers to their pension, funded by the companies making the money.
